Bluestripe herring (Herklotsichthys quadrimaculatus) attain an ultimate standard length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a relatively modest size for a clupeid of the Indo-Pacific region, reflecting the species' pelagic, fast-growing life style. Field surveys across the central Philippines have consistently recorded maximum sizes within this range, with adults rarely exceeding this asymptotic dimension. Egg diameter data, primarily derived from the closely related congener Spratelloides gracilis, indicate an average oocyte size of approximately 0.45 millimeters, which when incorporated into volumetric estimates yields a calculated wet weight at birth of around 0.000048 grams [Wwb = around 0.000048 grams]. This minute birth mass places the newly hatched yolk-sac larva among the smallest of the regional clupeids, a trait that imposes substantial vulnerability during the early, endotrophic phase of development when the larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves prior to the onset of exogenous feeding.

Pubertal development in Bluestripe herring is initiated once individuals reach a standard length of 10.1 centimeters [Lp = 10.1 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds roughly to the point at which gonadal recrudescence becomes histologically detectable. This size at sexual maturity is relatively small compared to the maximum attainable length, implying a life-history strategy that favors early reproductive investment over extended somatic growth. Under the thermal conditions typical of tropical surface waters, where ambient temperatures hover near 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the species exhibits a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 548 days [am = approximately 548 days]. This abbreviated longevity, less than two years, is characteristic of many small, fast-growing clupeids and is tightly linked to the high metabolic demands imposed by consistently warm environments, which accelerate physiological aging and senescent decline.

The maximum recorded longevity of 1.5 years [am = 1.5 years] in Bluestripe herring underscores its status as a short-lived, rapid-turnover forage fish within coral reef and coastal ecosystems at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This lifespan, documented from otolith-based age validation studies conducted at a mean water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], is consistent with the r-selected demographic profile typical of the genus Herklotsichthys. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, estimated from length–weight regressions fitted to large sample series, reaches an asymptotic mass of 202 grams [Wwi = 202 grams] in fully grown individuals. This body mass, though modest, supports the species' role as a critical trophic link, transferring pelagic primary and secondary production to higher-level piscivores such as tunas, jacks, and seabirds.

Reproductive output in Bluestripe herring is characterized by a high fecundity that compensates for the brief adult lifespan. Gravid females produce approximately 319 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 319 eggs per spawning event], and spawning occurs with a frequency of about 202 events per year [F_R_i = about 202 events per year] under prevailing thermal regimes of 28.5 °C. This extraordinary spawning frequency, essentially a daily or near-daily batch-spawning pattern, maximizes lifetime reproductive success in an environment where egg and larval mortality rates are exceptionally high. The combination of modest clutch size and extreme iteroparity is an adaptation that buffers against stochastic variation in planktonic food availability and predation pressure during the vulnerable pelagic larval phase, ensuring that at least some cohorts encounter favorable conditions for survival.

Comparative analysis with other small clupeids endemic to the Indo-Pacific indicates that Bluestripe herring's life-history syndrome—fast growth, early maturation, high reproductive effort, and abbreviated longevity—is finely tuned to the warm, productive, but highly variable conditions of tropical neritic waters. The newly hatched larva, with an estimated wet weight of just 0.000048 grams [Wwb = 0.000048 grams], faces a critical period of high starvation risk before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. Yet the species' ability to sustain such a high reproductive load at 28.5 °C, combined with a generation time of less than one year, enables rapid population turnover and resilience to harvesting pressure. These traits make H. quadrimaculatus a classic example of a short-lived, highly fecund pelagic spawner whose demographic parameters are governed more by environmental stochasticity than by density-dependent regulation.
